title: Boundary Kerr Signatures of the Interband-Coherence Hall Effect
abstract: We identify a Hall response carried by optically induced interband coherence rather than by a non-equilibrium band population. In a weakly doped zinc-blende semiconductor, a longitudinal dc field drives a transverse flux of the conduction--valence coherence created by near-gap light. Angular averaging eliminates the homogeneous coherence density, while a lateral boundary converts the transverse flux into an antisymmetric, edge-localized, helicity-odd polarization. The resulting Kerr signal requires neither spin-orbit coupling nor a spin, valley, or orbital accumulation within an individual band. Within the eight-band Kane model, we derive the boundary kinetic equation and obtain a complex propagation length controlled by optical detuning and interband dephasing. The edge profile is monotonic at optical resonance and develops damped spatial oscillations away from it. The response is enhanced by electron--hole asymmetry and by strong interband mixing, making narrow-gap semiconductors especially favorable to observe the effect. These results establish dc-driven Kerr microscopy as a direct probe of an interband-coherence Hall effect and of multiband quantum kinetics in real space.
summary: This theoretical work establishes a direct method—dc-driven Kerr microscopy—to probe an interband-coherence Hall effect in semiconductors. It shows that applying a DC field generates a transverse coherence flux, which manifests as a measurable, edge-localized polarization signal at physical boundaries. This mechanism is fundamentally distinct from traditional spin or orbital effects.
main_problem: The study identifies a novel Hall response mechanism driven by optically induced interband coherence, distinct from conventional non-equilibrium band population effects.
main_result: A dc electric field drives a transverse flux of conduction-valence coherence, which is converted into an antisymmetric, edge-localized Kerr signal at boundaries. This effect requires no spin-orbit coupling or intra-band accumulation.
method: The analysis involves deriving and solving boundary kinetic equations for the interband coherence density and flux using the eight-band Kane model framework.
model_or_system: The system is a weakly doped zinc-blende semiconductor, modeled using the eight-band Kane Hamiltonian. The dynamics are governed by coupled drift-diffusion equations describing the evolution of optical coherence.
key_observables: Kerr signal ($\Theta_K$, $\eta_K$), interband coherence flux ($J_L^y$), and coherence density ($L$).
important_parameters: Optical detuning ($\delta_F$), interband dephasing length ($\ell_\phi$), electron–hole asymmetry, and semiconductor band gap structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a two-moment closure approximation for the coherence dynamics; specific boundary conditions (diffusive/specular) are applied to model reflection at interfaces.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conversion of interband coherence flow into an edge Kerr signal, showing monotonic resonance profiles and damped spatial oscillations away from resonance due to detuning.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical mechanism (coherence flux driven by DC field), deriving the necessary kinetic equations using the Kane model, solving these equations under boundary conditions, and finally analyzing the resulting spectral and spatial dependence of the Kerr signal.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state transport, the rigorous derivation of coherence dynamics and its coupling to boundary effects mirrors complex open quantum system problems where boundary conditions dictate observable macroscopic responses.

The dc field Edcˆx drives its transverse flux JL y toward the side walls. The boundary normal ±ˆy converts this flux into opposite helicity- odd edge polarizations, which rotate the reflected polarization by ΘK. The response is bilinear in the optical and dc fields and is not a spin or orbital population accumulation.

FIG. 2. Coherent edge propagation revealed by optical detuning. Normalized Kerr angle (solid lines) and elliptic- ity (dashed lines) profiles are shown versus distance. The resonant signal decays monotonically, whereas detuning gives the propagation length in Eq. (15) an imaginary part and pro- duces damped sign changes. Such oscillations are absent from a purely relaxational spin-diffusion profile. The slab thickness W = 10 uFτϕ.
